after: ## Why there are two approaches at all
alt: Positivism and interpretivism compared. Positivism, linked to Comte and Durkheim, takes a macro view, uses the scientific method and quantitative data, and tends to be reliable but may lack validity. Interpretivism, linked to Weber, takes a micro view, seeks verstehen through qualitative data, and tends to be valid but may lack reliability.
caption: Each approach starts from a different view of people, which leads to a different idea of good evidence.

after: ## The key terms explained through one example
alt: The topic of early school leaving seen through two lenses. The positivist lens finds patterns, trends and correlations objectively and tends to be reliable but may lack validity. The interpretivist lens explores meanings with some subjectivity and tends to be valid but may lack reliability.
caption: Positivist research tends to be reliable; interpretivist research tends to be valid.

after: ## Correlation and causation: three reasons a link can mislead
alt: Three panels. A third factor: parental income or education may cause both owning more books and higher grades. Reverse direction: unemployment and poor mental health are linked, but poor health might cause job loss. Chance or a small sample: a pattern found in one school may disappear in a larger study.
caption: Two things moving together does not prove that one causes the other.

alt: Eileen Barker’s study The Making of a Moonie (1984) used participant observation, in-depth interviews and a large questionnaire to investigate why people joined and left the Unification Church. Triangulation uses methods to cross-check each other; methodological pluralism uses them to build a fuller picture.
caption: Barker combined three methods so each could check the others.

alt: The same group of people is studied in four waves over time, and some drop out at each wave (attrition). Longitudinal studies show sequence, helping move from correlation towards causation, but they are costly, lose sample members, need long-term funding and may change participants’ behaviour.
caption: Following the same people over time shows what came first.

alt: Seven evaluation concepts with a meaning and an example of a cause in the design: bias, interviewer effect, Hawthorne or observer effect, validity and reliability, plus representativeness, which is needed for generalisability.
caption: Name the concept, then link it to a cause in the design.

alt: A three-step evaluate answer. For: interviews give verstehen and validity. Against: small samples limit representativeness, generalisability and reliability, while positivism shows patterns at scale. Judgement: usefulness depends on the research aim, and triangulation combines both.
caption: For, against, then a judgement linked to the research aim.

alt: Four command words. Define: one accurate sentence with an example. Explain: develop a point with because and apply it. Discuss: several developed points in paragraphs. Evaluate: argue both sides with evaluation concepts and reach a judgement. Question 1(e) asks you to justify a plan, not evaluate it.
caption: Match the depth of your answer to the command word.
